tldr: This paper presents FA-RDP, a frequency-adaptive reactive diffusion policy for contact-rich manipulation. It dynamically switches its inference frequency to combine diverse pre-contact motion generation with rapid post-contact force feedback responses. In three real-robot tasks, FA-RDP achieved an average success rate of 81.7%, significantly outperforming existing methods.
hero_caption: Conceptual diagram of adaptive inference frequency switching across task phases. Before contact, a low-frequency (10 Hz) multi-step sampler preserves the diversity (multimodality) of multiple approach trajectories. After contact, where physical constraints narrow the solution space, the policy switches to a distilled high-frequency (30 Hz) one-step sampler to deliver rapid force responses.
overview:
In contact-rich manipulation, a single episode contains two phases with fundamentally different requirements. In the pre-contact phase, multiple approach trajectories might exist to reach the object while avoiding obstacles, requiring the policy to preserve action multimodality. In the post-contact phase, geometric constraints and force limits narrow the solution space, making rapid, millisecond-level reactivity to force (wrench) feedback essential to prevent slips, disengagement, or excessive force.

However, standard diffusion policies operate with fixed sampling steps and inference frequencies throughout an episode. Running low-frequency control with multi-step denoising preserves pre-contact diversity but responds too slowly to force changes. Conversely, high-frequency control accelerated via distillation collapses pre-contact trajectories into a single mode. This presents a fundamental tradeoff.

To resolve this tradeoff, the authors introduce FA-RDP, which dynamically switches inference frequency based on the situation. A shared multi-frequency visual-force Transformer handles both low and high frequencies using frequency-adaptive positional encodings. A learned multimodality indicator selects the sampler based on action ambiguity. In addition, Manifold Consistency Distillation (MCD) stabilizes one-step high-frequency control after contact.

Evaluated on three contact-rich manipulation tasks using a dual-arm real robot, FA-RDP achieved an average success rate of 81.7%, outperforming baselines by 30.0 percentage points. It successfully demonstrated both the flexibility to select among diverse pre-contact paths and agile, smooth post-contact force control.
contributions: Proposed FA-RDP, a visual-force diffusion policy that dynamically switches between a low-frequency multi-step sampler and a high-frequency one-step sampler based on a multimodality indicator, addressing the distinct requirements before and after contact.

Unified low- and high-frequency action prediction within a single Transformer backbone via frequency-adaptive positional encodings that assign sparse or dense position indices along a shared continuous time grid.

Introduced Manifold Consistency Distillation (MCD), which predicts actions directly on the robot action manifold rather than in noise space while retaining residual supervision, enabling stable one-step high-frequency inference.
Demonstrated an 81.7% average success rate across three contact-rich tasks on real dual-arm robots while preserving diverse pre-contact trajectory modes.

sections.heading: Diversity before contact, reactivity after: How can we resolve this fundamental tradeoff?
sections.summary: Contact-rich manipulation requires both preserving trajectory diversity before contact and providing rapid reactivity to force feedback after contact. Fixed-frequency diffusion policies cannot satisfy both. This work solves this problem using dynamic frequency adaptation driven by a multimodality indicator alongside a new distillation technique.
sections.details:
Contact-rich robotic manipulation involves two phase-dependent challenges. Before contact, multiple valid options (multimodality) exist, such as choosing whether to approach around the left or right side of an obstacle. The policy must preserve these diverse modes. Once contact occurs, physical constraints narrow valid motions, and slight pose errors cause excessive impact forces, slipping, or loss of contact. Rapid closed-loop responses driven by force feedback become crucial.

Standard diffusion policies predict temporally coherent action chunks, but execution within each chunk is largely open-loop. Hierarchical models (such as RDP) lose spatial details through compressed latent representations between layers. End-to-end approaches like ImplicitRDP limit the frequency of force updates due to the computational cost of multi-step denoising.

Could we simply distill the model down to a one-step denoising sampler? Relying on one-step generation across the entire episode introduces a critical failure mode: it tends to collapse pre-contact multimodal distributions or produce jerky motions that break contact. We need a mechanism that adaptively uses multi-step low-frequency sampling before contact to preserve diversity, then transitions to high-frequency one-step sampling after contact.

FA-RDP realizes this concept. In real-robot experiments, it achieved an average success rate of 81.7%, outperforming baselines (including ImplicitRDP) by 30.0 percentage points.

After contact, geometric constraints narrow the valid solution space, triggering a switch to a high-frequency distilled sampler.

sections.heading: Force-guided learning, multi-frequency policies, and distillation: Three lines of work
sections.summary: The paper builds on robot learning with force inputs, multi-frequency control, and diffusion distillation techniques. FA-RDP synthesizes these directions into an adaptive framework guided by task phase requirements.
sections.details:
Related work spans three primary categories:

- Robot Learning with Force Input:
Vision-only policies (such as Diffusion Policy and ACT) cannot process instantaneous contact forces, making them fragile in contact-rich settings. Incorporating force or tactile conditioning and adding hierarchical low-latency controllers helped, but open-loop gaps or information loss in compressed intermediate representations remained. FA-RDP achieves adaptive frequency within a single, end-to-end network.

- Multi-Frequency Policy Learning:
Hierarchical architectures that plan globally at low frequencies while executing reactive control at high frequencies, as well as asynchronous sensing pipelines, have been explored before. However, prior work focused primarily on hierarchical control or handling asynchronous sensors. FA-RDP introduces an adaptive design explicitly driven by the physical phase transition between pre-contact multimodality and post-contact force reactivity.

- Robot Policy Distillation:
To reduce diffusion sampling steps, DDIM, progressive distillation, consistency models, and flow-based approaches (such as MeanFlow) have been adapted for robotics. However, directly distilling noise ($\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$), scores, or velocity vectors into a student network often leads to severe training instability in robot action spaces. FA-RDP resolves this by reparameterizing the problem to predict directly on the robot action manifold.

sections.heading: Background: Consistent reactive denoising inference
sections.summary: ImplicitRDP established a way to handle visual tokens and high-rate force tokens inside a single Transformer. It provides closed-loop control across action chunks using causal masking and deterministic DDIM sampling, but multi-step denoising limits its inference frequency.
sections.details:
FA-RDP builds upon the consistent reactive denoising mechanism introduced in end-to-end visual-force diffusion models. In this formulation, slow-rate context tokens (vision and proprioception) and high-density fast tokens (force-torque measurements) are concatenated and processed in a single Transformer.

During training, a causal action-force mask prevents action tokens at time step $t$ from attending to future force tokens. This enables parallel diffusion training while preventing future contact information leaks.

During inference, slow context tokens and initial noise $\mathbf{A}_K$ are cached at the start of each action chunk. By applying deterministic DDIM ($\eta=0$), the policy updates its trajectory conditioning on newly arrived force tokens without introducing stochastic path deviations. However, running multi-step denoising at every control cycle limits the closed-loop frequency, restricting reactivity during rapid contact dynamics.

sections.heading: Inside FA-RDP: Multi-frequency Transformer, indicator, and manifold distillation
sections.summary: FA-RDP consists of three core components: a multi-frequency Transformer sharing a single backbone, a multimodality indicator for phase switching, and Manifold Consistency Distillation (MCD) for stable one-step high-frequency control. A 100 Hz force compensation layer further improves tracking.
sections.details:
FA-RDP is organized into three training stages (Stage 1 to 3):

- IV-A Multi-Frequency Visual-Force Transformer (Stage 1):
Instead of maintaining separate models for low and high frequencies, FA-RDP uses a single shared backbone. The core design is frequency-adaptive positional encoding (Fig. F2). Frequency modes are not distinguished by extra tokens. Instead, they share a continuous time grid with varying index steps: dense consecutive indices for 30 Hz and sparse strides (step of 3) for 10 Hz, covering the same 1.6-second duration with fully shared weights. Causal masking prevents future information leakage. The network is parameterized to directly predict the action chunk $\hat{\mathbf{A}}^\nu$ using DDPM residual supervision.

- IV-B Multimodality-Guided Frequency Selection (Stage 2):
Without relying on manual phase labels, an indicator head predicts action ambiguity from visual features using an independent calibration dataset. It is trained to estimate the dispersion (residual) observed across $N=8$ repeated samples drawn from the frozen Stage 1 model with different initial noises. At inference, when this estimated ambiguity drops below a threshold, the system infers that physical constraints have narrowed the action distribution and switches to high-frequency mode.

- IV-C Manifold Consistency Distillation for One-Step Control (MCD, Stage 3):
Multi-step sampling remains too slow for high-frequency mode. Consistency distillation solves this, but FA-RDP formulates distillation directly on the robot action manifold rather than in noise space (Fig. F3). By combining a consistency loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MCD}}$ between student and EMA teacher predictions with a supervised residual loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SRL}}$ on demonstration actions, the policy avoids mode collapse and achieves stable one-step execution.

- IV-D Implementation Details:
Low-frequency mode operates at 10 Hz (prediction horizon $H_\ell=16$), and high-frequency mode runs at 30 Hz ($H_h=48$), both covering 1.6 seconds. Inference latency on an RTX 5090 is under 30 ms for high frequency and under 50 ms for low frequency. To compensate for robot impedance tracking delays, all methods include a 100 Hz translational force compensation layer using current wrench readings.

captions.F2: Architecture of the multi-frequency visual-force Transformer. Across a shared continuous time grid, high-frequency (30 Hz) actions use consecutive dense indices, while low-frequency (10 Hz) actions use sparse indices, allowing a single model to share weights across both action chunk frequencies.
captions.F3: Overview of Manifold Consistency Distillation (MCD). Predictions from the student and EMA teacher networks are aligned directly on the robot action manifold rather than in noise space, combined with a supervised residual loss (SRL) on demonstrations to stabilize high-frequency one-step action prediction.

sections.heading: Real-robot evaluations: Outperforming baselines while preserving diversity and reactivity
sections.summary: FA-RDP was evaluated across three dual-arm real-robot tasks: Dual Box Flipping, Dual Switch Toggling, and Dual Button Pressing. Achieving an 81.7% average success rate, FA-RDP demonstrated both pre-contact trajectory diversity and stable post-contact force control, while baselines suffered from contact disengagement and collisions.
sections.details:
The experimental platform used two Flexiv Rizon 4s arms equipped with wrist F/T sensors, wrist cameras (iPhone fisheye), and a third-person camera (Fig. F4). Three tasks were designed with two foreground blocks creating multiple valid approach paths (left, right, or center). 60 demonstrations were collected per task, followed by 20 evaluation trials.

- Q1: Comparison with Baselines (Table I)
The tasks were Dual Box Flipping, Dual Switch Toggling, and Dual Button Pressing. FA-RDP achieved the highest performance across all tasks, averaging an 81.7% success rate (compared to 51.7% for ImplicitRDP, 36.7% for hierarchical RDP, 11.7% for vision-only DP, and 0.0% for direct regression). Failure mode analysis (Figs. F5, F6, F7) showed that DP and ImplicitRDP lost contact due to delayed force reactivity, RDP suffered pose offsets from latent policy compression, and direct regression averaged multimodal pre-contact paths into central collisions with obstacles. FA-RDP maintained contact throughout execution.

- Q2: Preserving Multimodality
Categorizing approach paths into four spatial modes revealed that the high-frequency distilled model collapsed entirely into a single mode. In contrast, FA-RDP distributed approaches evenly across all four modes, matching ImplicitRDP and confirming that multi-step low-frequency sampling preserves trajectory diversity.

- Q3: Effectiveness of Indicator-Guided Switching (Table II, Fig. F9)
Compared to running the high-frequency distilled model continuously (61.7% success rate), switching adaptively from low to high frequency via the multimodality indicator boosted success to 81.7%. As shown in Fig. F9, the indicator value remains low during pre-contact approach and quickly exceeds the threshold (3.5) when contact forces emerge, cleanly triggering high-frequency one-step control.

- Q4: Distillation Comparison (Table III)
In high-frequency mode, running the undistilled model in one step or using existing distillation methods (MeanFlow Policy, Consistency Policy) led to near-total failure (1.7% average success rate). By contrast, MCD achieved 61.7%, underscoring the necessity of distilling directly on the robot action manifold.

sections.heading: Conclusions and outlook: Frequency adaptation for precise contact manipulation
sections.summary: FA-RDP resolves the conflict between diversity and reactivity in contact-rich tasks through phase-adaptive frequencies and manifold distillation. While current limitations include task-specific training and a three-stage pipeline, the approach offers a strong foundation for future robot policies.
sections.details:
FA-RDP successfully reconciles two conflicting control requirements: preserving pre-contact trajectory diversity and providing millisecond-level reactivity to post-contact force feedback. Combining a shared multi-frequency Transformer, indicator-driven switching, and Manifold Consistency Distillation (MCD) yielded an 81.7% task success rate on physical hardware.

The authors also outline several current limitations. The framework was evaluated solely on vision and force-torque inputs, leaving integration with high-resolution tactile arrays or proximity sensing for future work. Furthermore, policies are trained per-task rather than as a multi-task policy, and training requires three sequential stages: multi-frequency pretraining, indicator calibration, and consistency distillation.

takeaways: In contact-rich robotic tasks, pre-contact multimodal exploration and post-contact reactive control have fundamentally different sampling requirements; forcing an entire episode into a single frequency or step budget creates an inherent tradeoff.

When distilling diffusion policies for robotics, predicting noise or velocity vectors often causes severe instability; distilling consistency directly on the robot action manifold with supervised residual regularization (MCD) proves far more reliable.

Representing multiple action chunk frequencies via sparse versus dense indices along a shared continuous time grid—rather than adding frequency conditioning tokens—provides an elegant, unified Transformer architecture without extra parameters.

Using internal sampling variance to self-estimate action ambiguity (the multimodality indicator) and using it to trigger control mode switches is a versatile design pattern applicable to other policy learning architectures.
limitations: The training pipeline involves three separate stages (multi-frequency policy training, indicator head calibration, and MCD distillation), which is more complex than end-to-end single-stage workflows.
Experiments are limited to vision and force-torque sensing; compatibility with other modalities like high-density tactile skins or proximity sensors has not been tested.
Evaluations were conducted on single-task policies; scaling the framework to large multi-task policies or vision-language-action (VLA) foundation models remains open.
